title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

reading.body:
Scammers impersonated Terry Gross and other NPR personalities to solicit fees from people seeking interviews on Fresh Air. The fraudulent emails were highly personalized, referencing victims' work and creating fake booking processes that mimicked legitimate ones. The scam worked because artificial intelligence made the impersonations and personalization convincing enough that victims initially believed they were authentic.

This is an impersonation attack deployed at scale against a well-known public figure and institution. It did not require access to Fresh Air's systems or email infrastructure. WHYY and NPR received multiple complaints and confirmed the fraud, but it is not established how many people paid or the total financial harm. The scam could have been caught if victims had verified requests using contact information from Fresh Air's official website rather than replying to the fraudulent messages.

It is not established whether the scammers used a specific AI system, how the system was prompted or trained, or what role AI played beyond making the messages more convincing.

reports.title: ‘Too good to be true?’: No, WHYY’s Terry Gross did not personally email you to be a guest on ‘Fresh Air’
Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

summary:
# Summary

Scammers are impersonating Terry Gross and other NPR personalities to defraud people seeking interviews on the popular radio program "Fresh Air." The fraudsters send highly personalized emails to authors, entertainers and public figures, referencing their work and creating fake booking processes. Several victims, including Misericordia University history professor Jennifer M. Black, initially believed the invitations were legitimate before being asked to pay fees ranging from around $250 for supposed production costs. WHYY, NPR and the show have confirmed receiving multiple complaints and are investigating with law enforcement.

Cybersecurity experts say artificial intelligence has made these scams more convincing and personalized than traditional fraud attempts. WHYY emphasized it never charges guests for interviews and stated any communication requesting payment should be treated as fraudulent. Red flags include emails from suspicious addresses like "terrygrossfreshair@gmail.com" and requests for money. Experts advise recipients to verify requests directly with the organization through legitimate contact information rather than responding to suspicious messages.
